digests.standfirst: For the first time the whole United Nations membership has agreed that a state does not stop being a state when its territory goes under water, and that its ocean boundaries hold where its coastline does not — and the United States did not block it. In the same week NATO published the first revision of its resilience baseline in a decade, with extreme weather written in and the words climate change written out, while a British foreign secretary told the security community that climate belongs in threat assessments and then routed £1 million of a £331 million package to the only standing multilateral machinery the field has. Somalia's government and the United Nations asked for money to act on a flood forecast that is about as close to certain as forecasts get, and did not get it.

The attribution scientists who spent three weeks declining to say whether warming caused the Himalayan disaster published on 17 September and did something neither side of that argument expected: they refused the event-level question, attributed the conditions that produced it, and declared the event past the limits of what adaptation could have prevented. Within twenty-four hours Nepal's finance minister was in New Delhi using the finding. Meanwhile the Dutch budget answered a request to double water spending by funding the one thing the request said was already funded, and the United States finalised the repeal of its power-plant carbon rules on the floor of a G20 energy meeting whose only outcome document does not contain the word climate.

The UN's climate secretariat takes the security frame to the European Parliament and calls the summer a continent-wide economic security emergency; the Netherlands' delta commissioner asks the cabinet to double water spending to two per cent of GDP and says plainly that not all damage can now be prevented; and Nepal puts a $4.78 billion reconstruction bill to the world in the same week its scientists agree publicly that they cannot attribute the disaster that caused it.

The UN Environment Programme concedes that 1.5°C will be crossed and asks governments to manage the overshoot instead; small island states and Pacific leaders refuse the frame within forty-eight hours; and a Himalayan disaster turns into an argument about which monitoring system should have caught it.

Two multilateral instruments fail in one week, the military climate-security reporting infrastructure is found to have quietly stopped publishing, and attribution claims run wrong in both directions on two different disasters.
